article_title: Firefox 159 Enables Scroll-Driven Animations by Default and Adds Scoped Custom Element Registries; web.dev Lists Both as Baseline Newly Available
summary: Approved after manual source verification. The script's APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS came only from the web.dev allowlist warning; web.dev was independently confirmed as Google's Chrome DevRel site and added to config/source_allowlist.txt, and every claim, quote, number and date traced to a snapshot.

findings.message: web.dev allowlist warning resolved by editorial confirmation
findings.details: web.dev/about states the site is 'brought to you by the Chrome DevRel team'; the developer.chrome.com snapshot links to web.dev in its Resources menu; web.dev/baseline states Baseline 'was originated by the Chrome team and is now defined by the WebDX Community Group'. Domain added to config/source_allowlist.txt with a justification comment in the same commit. It is a Google/Chrome property and not independent of Chrome.

Firefox 159 shipped on October 27, 2026 (11 days before review, web.dev post October 29), so the coverage is a roundup rather than breaking news. Title is 145 characters, under the 150-character guideline.

Two Mozilla first-party pages (MDN and firefox.com release notes). web.dev (Google Chrome DevRel), the Chrome for Developers blog (Google and Microsoft Edge team) and the WebKit blog (Apple) are other browser vendors' documentation, independent of Mozilla but not news outlets. Two DEV Community posts are individual authors' posts. No news-outlet coverage. News category requires 3-5 sources and has no independence minimum.

content_preview.title: Firefox 159 Enables Scroll-Driven Animations by Default and Adds Scoped Custom Element Registries; web.dev Lists Both as Baseline Newly Available
content_preview.summary: Firefox 159, released October 27, 2026, enables scroll-driven animations by default and adds scoped custom element registries, which web.dev lists as Baseline Newly available; legacy masonry syntax is removed.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Firefox 159 was released on October 27, 2026, according to [MDN's release notes for developers](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Mozilla/Firefox/Releases/159). The release enables scroll-driven animations by default and adds support for scoped custom element registries, both listed in the same notes. In its ["New to the web platform in October" post](https://web.dev/blog/web-platform-10-2026), published October 29, 2026, web.dev lists both features as Baseline Newly availabl...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear News roundup of 697 words (News range 400-1200) with a sensible structure: overview, one section per feature, other changes, and a closing 'What the sources do not say' section. Technical depth fits a web developer audience. Quotes are short and attributed, and author reports from the DEV posts are labelled as individual authors' accounts.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 7 snapshots were read from sources/2026-11/ (gunzip, HTML to text) and cross-checked against the article. source-0 (MDN Firefox 159 notes): 'Firefox 159 was released on October 27, 2026.' confirmed; 'Scroll-driven animations are now enabled by default.' appears verbatim, followed by the description of a scroll-based timeline versus the default time-based document timeline; the 'Removals' entry for legacy masonry syntax (masonry value of grid-template-columns/rows, masonry-auto-flow, Nightly-only behind a preference, superseded by grid lanes with grid-lanes and inline-grid-lanes display values) matches the article; scoped registries are listed under DOM as 'now supported' (independent CustomElementRegistry for a DOM subtree, customElementRegistry property on Document, Element and ShadowRoot, CustomElementRegistry() constructor); the HTML Sanitizer API/Element.setHTML() entry matches. Scoped registries are NOT in the 'Experimental web features ... disabled by default' list for 159, consistent with the article. source-1 (firefox.com 159.0 release notes, 'Version 159.0, first offered to Release channel users on October 27, 2026'): the Web Platform entries list animation-timeline, scroll-timeline, view-timeline, animation-range, ScrollTimeline and ViewTimeline; 'Firefox now supports scoped custom element registries'; Web Console let/const/class redeclaration; WebGL EXT_clip_control, EXT_texture_mirror_clamp_to_edge and WebGL 2 EXT_texture_norm16 'on compatible devices' - all match. Note the firefox.com notes say 'supports' while only MDN says 'enabled by default' for scroll-driven animations; the article attributes the phrase to MDN. source-2 (web.dev 'New to the web platform in October', Rachel Andrew, Published: October 29, 2026, page title matches the article's quoted post name): both quotes are verbatim ('With support in Chrome, Safari, and now Firefox 159, scroll-driven animations are Baseline Newly available.'; 'Previously, all custom elements had to be registered in a single global window.customElements registry, which could cause naming collisions when combining components from different libraries or teams.'; 'With support across Chrome, Safari, and Firefox 159, scoped custom element registries are now Baseline Newly available.'); the support tables, read from the image alt text in the raw HTML, are Chrome 115/Edge 115/Firefox 159/Safari 26 for scroll-driven animations and Chrome 146/Edge 146/Firefox 159/Safari 26 for scoped registries, as the article states. The title's Baseline Newly available claim is therefore directly supported. source-3 (Chrome for Developers, Published: March 9, 2026): the quote 'now available by default from Edge and Chrome 146, as well as other Chromium-based browsers' is verbatim (a line break splits it in the HTML); the prose supports exactly Chrome and Edge 146 and the article cites it for nothing more. source-4 (WebKit 'WebKit Features in Safari 26.0', Sep 15, 2025): names Scroll-driven animations in the intro and has a dedicated section, supporting 'names scroll-driven animations among the features arriving in that release'; it also says Safari 26.0 'now supports Scoped Custom Element Registry', which backs the DEV post's Safari 26.0 claim although the article cites WebKit only for scroll-driven animations. source-5 (DEV, richi.codes, Posted on Nov 4, datePublished 2026-11-04): the CSS.supports('animation-timeline: scroll()') check with a scroll listener and IntersectionObserver fallback, the overflow: hidden versus overflow: clip finding (reported as observed in Chromium), and the 'Baseline "newly available" means every engine ships it, not that every user has updated ... Keep the fallback for a while' advice all match. source-6 (DEV, JKC, Posted on Nov 7): 'Safari 26.0 shipped it first, and Safari 26.4 added upgrading elements in initialize() plus fixes around null registries', document.createElement() still using the global registry by default, and initialize() first come, first served (the root kept the first registry, 'one'), all match and are attributed to the author. No adoption figures appear in any cited source, so the closing statement is accurate. Suspicious-pattern scan: manifest suspicious_patterns null for all 7 sources; my own scan found only the standard 'Guidance for AI agents' llms.txt link tag in the DEV page head of source-5 and source-6, which is site boilerplate with no instruction text and was not acted on. No snapshot required a WebFetch fallback. Allowlist: developer.mozilla.org, firefox.com, developer.chrome.com, webkit.org and dev.to are listed; web.dev was not, and was confirmed independently as Google's Chrome DevRel site (web.dev/about: 'brought to you by the Chrome DevRel team'; the developer.chrome.com snapshot links to web.dev; web.dev/baseline: Baseline 'originated by the Chrome team and is now defined by the WebDX Community Group') and added to config/source_allowlist.txt in this review commit. Independent-source recount: 2 Mozilla pages are first-party to the subject (Firefox 159). Independent of Mozilla: web.dev, the Chrome blog and the WebKit blog (other browser vendors' documentation, not news outlets; web.dev and Chrome are both Google) plus 2 individual-author DEV posts. News requires 3-5 sources and no independence minimum, so the 7-source count is compliant; the Analysis rules do not apply.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every version, date, number, property name and quote traced to a snapshot. Firefox 159 release date October 27, 2026 confirmed by MDN and firefox.com. The Firefox 156 consistency check was done: the Herald's Firefox 156 article states per MDN's 156 notes that scoped custom element registries were disabled by default behind about:config (and enabled in Nightly), and the new article's description of that ('then disabled by default and had to be enabled through about:config') matches it; the 159 statement that they are now supported is consistent with that earlier coverage, and the 156 article link resolves to an existing article. No relative dates are used. The headline, summary and lead are each backed by cited sources. The 'Among other developer-facing items' list is framed as non-exhaustive. Every body URL is in article.sources and vice versa.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and factual, with no loaded language, no AI self-reference, and clear attribution of every claim to MDN, Mozilla, web.dev or the named DEV authors.
editor_notes.originality: New topic. The only related prior coverage is the Firefox 156 and 157 articles (scoped registries behind a flag in 156); no existing article covers Firefox 159, scroll-driven animations or Baseline Newly available status for these features, and no open PR duplicates it.
concerns: The sourcing is thin on independent reporting: the facts come from browser vendors' own documentation (Mozilla, Google, Apple) and two individual developers' blog posts, one of which (JKC) carries the line 'This article was written with the help of AI and checked against the sources above.' Those posts are used only for attributed author reports and for the Safari 26.4 detail, which no cited source corroborates beyond the author. This is acceptable for a News piece but means the Baseline status claim rests on Google's web.dev rather than on the WebDX or Mozilla sources.
The coverage is 11 days after the Firefox 159 release (October 27, 2026), so it is a roundup rather than breaking news.
recommendations: Where available, cite the web-features / Baseline status data directly (WebDX Community Group) in addition to web.dev for Baseline claims.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, well-sourced and neutral roundup; the headline's two Firefox claims and the web.dev Baseline claim are directly supported by the Mozilla and web.dev snapshots, all quotes are verbatim, and the Firefox 156 and 159 statements are consistent. Approved with web.dev added to the allowlist; no corrections needed. Featured candidacy: 1 - accurate Baseline milestone coverage for a defined web developer audience
